newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Thousands rally in Brussels against land mines.
newsitem.headline: Thousands rally in Brussels against land mines.

text.p: Thousands of people protested in Brussels against the use of land mines on Saturday ahead of a conference next week to prepare an international anti-mine treaty.
"The aim of this day is to raise public awareness about land mines," Susan Walker of French-Belgian Handicap International told Reuters on Saturday.
Behind her, dozens of old pairs of jeans, one leg cut off, hung on washing lines between the trees of Albertina square to symbolise the devastation caused by mines.

Handicap International, which provides artificial limbs for land mine victims worldwide, is one of more than a thousand non-governmental organisations (NGOs) who have joined the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL).
Founded in 1992, ICBL has put the use of anti-personnel mines on the world's agenda and is the driving force behind diplomatic efforts towards a treaty banning the use of mines.

"We want to stigmatise countries that still use mines, like others before us have stigmatised countries who used chemical or bacteriological weapons," said Chris Paul Giannou, a Red Cross war surgeon who has operated on hundreds of mine victims.
Every year 26,000 people die after stepping on landmines, and thousands more are maimed for life.
One of them is Opas Tiang Nok, a 32-year-old Thai. At 16, he stepped on a mine in a rice field close to the Thai-Cambodian border and lost his right leg.
Opas was one of 10 mine victims from Cambodia, Thailand, Angola, Mozambique and Bosnia who rode from Paris to Brussels on a hand-propelled tricycle to push for a ban on mines.
"I come here in the name of all the mine victims," he said.
Opas now works with Handicap International, producing prostheses for mine victims with local materials.

Cambodian Tun Channareth, who lost both his lower legs after stepping on a mine as a soldier, said he hoped the victims' presence in Brussels would help to convince world leaders to sign a ban on land mines.
Next week, delegations from about 140 countries are expected at the Brussels Conference on a Global Ban on Antipersonnel Mines.
The conference, which continues a series started in Ottawa, Canada last year, hopes to get at least 45 states to sign a treaty by the end of this year committing them to a total ban on landmines.

The U.S. is not taking part in the Ottawa-Brussels discussions -- although it will send observers to the conference -- preferring to seek a ban on mines via the U.N.-sponsored Conference on Disarmament in Geneva.
NGOs are sharply critical of the Clinton government's slow-track approach, since the need for consensus at the U.N. talks is likely to block a ban for years to come.
The U.S. refuses to give up using land mines as long as China and Russia, the main users and producers of mines, do not promise to do so as well.
